Q0312

“Nothing is miserable unless you think it so.” — Boethius (The Consolation of Philosophy II)

Verified English quotation. Primary source: The Consolation of Philosophy II. Theme: happiness.

Source and attribution

The archive attributes this English wording to The Consolation of Philosophy II and files it under Neoplatonism. That locator distinguishes the passage from loose internet attributions: readers can return to the named work or section to check translation, surrounding argument, and edition-specific wording.

About Boethius

Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524/5) was a Roman statesman and philosopher who translated Aristotle’s logic into Latin and wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison under Theodoric.

How to read this passage

Greek eudaimonia, Buddhist analyses of craving, utilitarian happiness, and modern well-being research all contest the meaning of a good life. This passage enters that discussion through happiness, mind.

Concepts in this quote

Happiness
Happiness—or flourishing—is a central aim in ethics: what makes a life go well, and whether pleasure alone is enough.
Mind
Philosophy of mind asks what consciousness, thought, and mental life are—and how they relate to body and world.
